enhanced.fullText:
The Copyright Act, codified at 17 U.S.C. §§ 101-1332, establishes comprehensive federal protection for original works of authorship fixed in tangible mediums, creating significant compliance obligations for higher education institutions. Under 17 U.S.C. § 106, copyright owners possess exclusive rights to reproduce, distribute, perform, display, and create derivative works from protected materials, including literary works, musical compositions, audiovisual content, sound recordings, and computer software.

Higher education institutions face particular scrutiny under the Act's enforcement provisions. Section 512 of the Digital Millennium Copyright Act (17 U.S.C. § 512) requires universities to implement DMCA compliance procedures, designate copyright agents with the U.S. Copyright Office, and maintain policies addressing repeat infringers to qualify for safe harbor protections. The Technology, Education and Copyright Harmonization (TEACH) Act, codified at 17 U.S.C. § 110(2), permits limited use of copyrighted materials in distance education but requires strict technological safeguards and institutional policies.

Fair use provisions under 17 U.S.C. § 107 provide qualified exceptions for educational purposes, considering four factors: purpose and character of use, nature of copyrighted work, amount used relative to the whole, and effect upon the work's market value. However, fair use determinations are highly fact-specific and do not guarantee protection for all educational activities.

Violations carry severe penalties under 17 U.S.C. § 504, including actual damages, profits from infringement, or statutory damages ranging from $750 to $150,000 per work for willful infringement. Criminal penalties under 17 U.S.C. § 506 may apply for willful infringement at commercial scale. The Higher Education Opportunity Act of 2008 (20 U.S.C. § 1094) requires institutions to develop plans for deterring unauthorized distribution of copyrighted materials and offer legal alternatives to illegal downloading. Universities must also comply with software licensing agreements and maintain accurate inventories of licensed software to avoid Business Software Alliance audits and potential litigation.
enhanced.summary: The Copyright Act protects original works of authorship and requires higher education institutions to implement DMCA compliance procedures, maintain copyright policies, respect fair use limitations, and develop plans to deter unauthorized distribution of protected materials.
enhanced.requirements:
## DMCA Compliance Infrastructure
- Designate and register copyright agent with U.S. Copyright Office under 17 U.S.C. § 512(c)(2)
- Implement notice-and-takedown procedures for reported infringements
- Maintain repeat infringer policies and enforcement mechanisms
- Establish technological safeguards for online content distribution

## Educational Use Policies
- Develop comprehensive copyright policies addressing fair use under 17 U.S.C. § 107
- Implement TEACH Act compliance for distance education per 17 U.S.C. § 110(2)
- Provide copyright training for faculty and staff
- Establish approval processes for copyrighted material usage

## Software License Management
- Maintain accurate inventories of all licensed software installations
- Implement procedures for software procurement and license compliance
- Conduct regular audits to ensure license compliance
- Establish centralized software asset management protocols

## Anti-Piracy Measures
- Develop plans to deter unauthorized distribution per 20 U.S.C. § 1094
- Implement network monitoring for copyright infringement
- Provide legal alternatives to illegal downloading
- Establish disciplinary procedures for policy violations
enhanced.reportingRequirements: No specific federal reporting requirements exist under the Copyright Act itself. However, institutions must respond to DMCA takedown notices within reasonable timeframes, typically 24-48 hours. Copyright agent contact information must be updated with the U.S. Copyright Office every three years or when changes occur.
